💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remember the tech boss and his head of HR, both married to other people, who were caught on camera at a Coldplay concert with their arms wrapped around each other?
  • Their horrified reaction went viral, and the pair both resigned.
  • Compared with the scandal which has engulfed Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in recent weeks, that Coldplay kiss cam moment now feels rather tame.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remember the tech boss and his head of HR, both married to other people, who were caught on camera at a Coldplay concert with their arms wrapped around each other?

Their horrified reaction went viral, and the pair both resigned. Astronomer, the firm where they both worked, mentioned their actions had fallen short of its standards.

Compared with the scandal which has engulfed Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in recent weeks, that Coldplay kiss cam moment now feels rather tame.

Huang admitted to having had an affair, reportedly with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

There were suggestions that she may have been involved in smuggling Nvidia chips into China, in breach of a US export ban.

Concerns about national security had reached the desk of US President Donald Trump.

There were other stories about some of Huang's relationships with female colleagues.

For most of us, that would without question amount to instant, and irreversible, dismissal.

But while Huang briefly left the firm, he was just as swiftly reinstated, and welcomed back with open arms.

As I watched footage of him being greeted with cheers, applause, high fives and a big hug back at the firm's HQ on Monday, I wondered how many disgraced bosses would kill to be in his shoes.

"Imagine being that Coldplay CEO reading all the comments on here about how it's OK if you're actually a good enough CEO," quipped menswear writer Derek Guy on X, external.

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO.

Huang has blown out of the water the old adage that nobody is irreplaceable.

Despite names of potential permanent replacements being bandied around, Nvidia's board evidently reached the same conclusion - interim chief executive Colette Kress was in for less than two weeks.

So how on Earth did he manage it?

Well firstly, Huang is the boss of a organization that has manoeuvred itself into a uniquely powerful position.

Nvidia's computer chips are considered the best in the business for driving AI.

Demand for its latest tech is through the roof and the firm sets its prices accordingly: Its Rubin and Vera GPUs sell for tens of thousands of dollars each, and one data centre might contain hundreds of them.

So, the US AI sector relies on Nvidia, Trump is determined that the American AI industry needs to be the best in the world, and Huang is the only leader the company has ever known.

He's been at the helm for 33 years and he's a computer scientist himself, renowned for being very hands-on with the development process. (Whether the boss's input is always wanted is another matter, but it's always there.).

Long hours are normal and negative feedback is often given in front of everyone else.

When he wants something to happen, he doesn't stop until it does: one of his early ideas was to halve the chip production cycle, in order to get one step ahead of the competition with their longer lead times for orders.

In a recent development, lots of experts told him it couldn't be done. Until eventually, they did it.

Not only does Huang have technical expertise, he's also a charismatic figurehead, representing Nvidia at events around the world in his trademark leather jacket, rubbing shoulders with world leaders, royalty, and fellow tech bosses.

For many, he's become something of a cult figure. Nvidia sometimes sells limited edition clothing at conference pop up stalls. A jumper featuring a cartoon image of Huang costs $178 (Â£137).

Nvidia's clothing lines quickly sell out, bought by fans of the tech giant.

In addition, Huang has powerful allies, and they are mostly powerful men. US President Donald Trump personally pushed for his return to Nvidia, while Elon Musk noted it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX.

He is one of very few people who knows both Trump and China's President Xi Jinping personally - and somehow he has surfed the geopolitical tension between the two continents.

He has said he thinks both China and the US can win the AI race and called on them to pull together.

And finally there's the bottom line, which is always money.

Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns.

Recent findings suggest that huang's brief departure from Nvidia caused economic turmoil. The firm's value sank by a whopping $1tn before it climbed back up again.

It affected not only pension funds and investors around the world, but also Nvidia's own staff.

Tech employees often get to own valuable stocks in the firm they work for as part of their pay packages.

According to recent reports, nvidia employees have been sitting on a goldmine. It wasn't really in their interests to see that drain away because of the boss's love life.

With a firm grip on the company he co-founded, cult-like status in tech circles and friends in high places, Jensen Huang created a situation where even national security concerns over the US's biggest rival couldn't topple him.

#3847. Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long

Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.
  • In a recent development, da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations.
  • Sources indicate that now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.

In a recent development, da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?

Sources indicate that now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” says Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.

Now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.

Sources indicate that “Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” notes Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”.

This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.

Recent findings suggest that but just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring newly introduced hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.

In September, the National Science Foundation announced a $30 million award to nine universities to stand up a new center dedicated to predicting turbulence—in the air, but also in the charged particles inside a fusion reactor, and in the gas clouds that stretch across space.

Sources indicate that “Turbulence is the reason we don’t have fusion energy yet,” says Murillo, who heads up the newly introduced center, called Transformative Explorations in Multi-Physics and Engineering of Scientific Turbulence, or Tempest. The chaotic swirling of superhot plasma inside a reactor allows heat to leak out, preventing the material from reaching the temperatures needed to allow nuclei to fuse. The US federal government wants to get closer to figuring that out.

Sources indicate that “Closer,” because turbulence is impossible to perfectly predict, scientists say. For one thing, turbulence occurs at many different, small scales at the same time. Air swirling around an airplane breaks into eddies, then smaller eddies, and then even smaller eddies, with each interacting with each other—too many variables, happening too quickly, to mathematically account for. For another, tiny changes—wind speed, temperature—can eventually dramatically alter air movement, suddenly altering the turbulence once predicted. To make perfect forecasts, one would need a perfect picture of exactly what’s going on in the atmosphere at all times.

But increasing sophisticated applications of machine learning could allow scientists to get closer to knowing what’s going to happen when, says Murillo. And while brute, computational force can’t solve the turbulence problem, AI agents might give the effort a boost. OpenAI’s blockbuster announcement this fall that it had resolved the Navier-Stokes problem—equations that are the beginning of all turbulence models—suggests LLMs could help.

“Turbulence has been a problem only human minds could work on; as of this year, that's no longer true,” indicates Murillo.

To make flying better, the aviation industry doesn’t necessarily need to solve turbulence. It needs to get better at knowing what sort of conditions create it and not send airplanes there.

Sources indicate that one tech giant in Tel Aviv, SkyPath, uses those in-plane iPads and their accelerometers to collect and share crowdsourced data between different airplanes, even if they don’t fly for the same airline. (This sort of dating sharing can be a sensitive topic for competing companies; SkyPath indicates it assuages these concerns by ensuring that data is anonymized before it’s shared.) More than 40,000 of these devices have SkyPath installed on them, says CEO Maya Shpak; the company says that several major airlines, including American, use the technology. SkyPath combines that collected data with additional information, including weather forecasts, and uses machine intelligence to make predictions about the future state of the air. The app helps pilots avoid turbulent air and warn passengers and crew members that choppiness is coming, 10 to 15 minutes before it happens.

Industry observers note that one pilot named Eric who uses SkyPath, who asked WIRED not to use his full name because he was not authorized to speak to the media, stated the app is a helpful tool that allows him to warn passengers what to expect. His issue is the same as those studying turbulence: One can’t take measurements everywhere all at once.

“It’s like any crowdsourced software,” says the pilot. “It only works if everyone uses it, and no one wants to use it until everyone else is.” Today, several large operators are using the app, which makes it especially useful in areas with lots of flights, he says.

Sources indicate that cornman, the physicist, wants to keep all these advances in perspective. “No matter what people say, we’re not getting close to 100 percent, 90 percent, 80 percent [predictive accuracy] anytime soon,” he notes. “It’s too complicated a problem.” Smoother skies, if not perfect ones, are ahead.

#3845. The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed

The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the organization faces.
  • Recent findings suggest that the central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances.
  • government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the organization faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models.

Recent findings suggest that the central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too.

The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.

In a recent development, diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine concern for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end owners of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch.

According to recent reports, and that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys stated, that would increase the tech giant’s legal risk.

“Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week.

The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a tech giant in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade.

On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued fresh rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls.

Sources indicate that nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance.

In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche mentioned that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week.

“When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche remarked.

Sources indicate that other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly, the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion.

Members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return. Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week. Teter reportedly intervened in the Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed last year.

“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of Nvidia products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” the Republican chairs of House committees focused on foreign affairs, intelligence, and China mentioned in a joint statement.

Recent findings suggest that rep. Brian Mast, the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has also demanded that the Department of Commerce share extensive data regarding its investigation into chip smuggling, including by Megaspeed and its affiliates.

The Senate Banking Committee will also question Huang in a public hearing on December 3.

Recent findings suggest that “Mr. Huang, Nvidia executives, and the firm’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democratic member on the committee, stated in a statement. “The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.”.

The best (and weirdest) Spotify Wrapped features through the years

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every year, Spotify Wrapped kicks off the same ritual: Instagram Stories fill up with top-five lists, friends compare how many minutes they spent listening, and someone has to explain how a song they swear they barely played ended up at No.
  • Sources indicate that over the years, Spotify has gotten a lot more creative with those numbers.
  • In 2023, Spotify Wrapped could tell you where in the world people listened to music just like you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every year, Spotify Wrapped kicks off the same ritual: Instagram Stories fill up with top-five lists, friends compare how many minutes they spent listening, and someone has to explain how a song they swear they barely played ended up at No. 1.

Sources indicate that over the years, Spotify has gotten a lot more creative with those numbers. It's turned listening habits into personality tests, matched people with cities they've never visited, and even stacked their favorite genres into a sandwich. With another Wrapped around the corner, we're looking back at the features that made us laugh, argue with our results, or wonder what exactly Spotify was thinking.

In 2023, Spotify Wrapped could tell you where in the world people listened to music just like you. The feature, called Sound Town, matched listeners with one of more than 1,300 places, from Provo, Utah, to Cuiabá, Brazil, to Burlington, Vermont. To get a match, at least three of your most-played artists had to be especially popular in the same city.

According to recent reports, the fun was finding out what else people in your Sound Town had on repeat. For example, SZA's "Kill Bill" was No. 1 in both Berkeley, California, and Cambridge, Massachusetts, and came in fifth in Jakarta, Indonesia. In Burlington, Vermont, Noah Kahan had four songs in the top 10. "Stick Season" was No. 1, naturally.

Once people started posting, a few cities, like Berkeley, Burlington, and Cambridge, took on a meaning of their own. Queer listeners comparing results noticed some familiar names in the mix, including boygenius, Charli XCX, and Janelle Monáe.

Spotify got in on it, tagging all three cities in a post, writing, "hey besties.".

It has been revealed that somehow, with this feature, a city you'd never set foot in could suddenly feel like a place where you knew people, even if all you'd shared was a playlist. — Olivia Tauber.

It has been revealed that spotify Wrapped added an aura reading in 2021. For Audio Aura, Spotify worked with aura reader Mystic Michaela to turn the two moods that highlighted up most in a listener's streaming history into a colorful, shareable card. The more someone listened to music in a particular mood, the darker its shade appeared.

It has been revealed that each color stated something about what people reached for when they put on music. Blue was for listeners who wanted to sit with their feelings, orange was for those who needed a confidence boost, and pink was for the hopeless romantics. The cards also spelled out the moods behind the colors, with labels like "blissful" and "chill.".

In a recent development, when Wrapped dropped on Dec. 1, listeners started posting their Audio Auras on Twitter. One user took their "chill and euphoric" result as confirmation that they had excellent taste and were, in fact, the hottest person ever.

By the next day, BuzzFeed had made a quiz predicting your 2022 aura. Later that month, Spotify built full-size pods based on the cards' color combinations for its Wrapped party, where Mystic Michaela gave guests in-person aura readings. Cute! — OT.

According to recent reports, one of Spotify's weirdest experiments was a podcast with an audience of one. Built with Google's NotebookLM, the Wrapped AI Podcast turned your listening stats into a conversation between two AI hosts. They addressed you by name, talked through your most-played songs and artists, and guessed what you might have been doing while you listened. After a year of hearing other people talk on Spotify, you could finally listen to an episode about you.

According to recent reports, the guesses were where things got weird. For example, when Gizmodo's Florence Ion tried it at the time, the hosts wondered whether her longest listening day had been a road trip. (She'd actually spent it crying and playing sad music.).

When Wrapped dropped on Dec. 4, some listeners actually complained that Spotify had put too much emphasis on the AI podcast. They missed the human touch of features of past. — OT.

Industry observers note that if you've ever taken a personality test and immediately made the results your entire identity, Spotify Wrapped 2022 had something for you. That year, Spotify introduced Your Listening Personality, assigning listeners one of 16 personality types based on their relationship with music.

Recent findings suggest that much like the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI), Spotify's personality test measured four different characteristics: Familiarity vs. Exploration, Timelessness vs. Newness, Loyalty vs. Variety, and Commonality vs. Uniqueness. Each listener received a four-letter combination and a corresponding personality.

Even the artists got in on it. Charli XCX was classified as a Specialist, which she told Spotify made sense, given that her attention was hard to capture but once it had it, she was committed. (She also revealed that she'd listened to Will Smith's "Miami" roughly 200 times that year.).

According to recent reports, the feature arrived at a time when the internet's appetite for personality tests seemed insatiable. Why stop at your zodiac sign, your MBTI, and your Enneagram when you could add a Spotify-assigned personality to your bio? For the record, I'm an ENVC. — Crystal Bell.

In a recent development, were you in your "Pink Pilates Princess Strut Pop" era or your "Sweater Weather Softcore Indie" era? These were actual things Spotify wanted you to consider in 2024.

It has been revealed that that year, Spotify introduced Your Music Evolution, a feature that divided your year into as many as three distinct musical phases. Spotify considered when your interest in certain artists and genres peaked, how much time you spent listening to them, and how significantly those habits deviated from your usual tastes.

The resulting labels sounded like someone had fed a year's worth of TikTok aesthetics into a musical Mad Libs generator. There was "Surf Crush Beach Reggae" and "Wild West Slow Dance Country," among countless other combinations. April was my "Pumpkin Spice Roller Skating Pop" season, which felt like a personal assault on my taste.

In a year when seemingly everything had become an aesthetic, from the way we dressed to the way we decorated our bedrooms, it felt appropriate that our listening habits got the same treatment.

Sources indicate that were these legitimate musical genres? Not exactly. Did they sound suspiciously like something you'd find on a Pinterest mood board? Absolutely. — CB.

In 2025, Spotify gave listeners a new reason to have an existential crisis: their Listening Age. The feature was inspired by a psychological phenomenon known as the reminiscence bump, the idea that people tend to form particularly strong attachments to music from their formative years.

According to recent reports, to calculate your Listening Age, Spotify examined the release years of the songs you streamed, identifying a five-year period of music you listened to disproportionately often compared with other people your age. It then assumed you would have been between 16 and 21 when that music came out.

Someone with an affinity for late-'70s music, for example, could receive a Listening Age of 63, regardless of their actual age. Naturally, some people felt called out.

Of course, you don't have to have lived through a particular musical era to feel nostalgic for it. Younger generations regularly discover decades-old songs through TikTok, television soundtracks, and their parents' record collections.

Sources indicate that it's easy to see why Listening Age was a hit with owners. The opportunity to receive a completely unnecessary personal assessment and immediately make it everyone else's business is part of what makes Spotify Wrapped so irresistible. And there's something particularly funny about a 22-year-old proudly announcing that they have the music taste of a 65-year-old as if it's some kind of cultural flex. — CB.

According to recent reports, remember the peak of the internet's main character era? In 2021, TikTok encouraged us to romanticize our lives, and Spotify gave us the soundtrack to do it.

With 2021: The Movie, Spotify assigned some of your most-played songs to scenes in a fictional movie starring you. There was a song for your opening credits, a dramatic declaration of love, a showdown with a rival dance crew, and even a battle against a supernatural villain. In my 2021 Wrapped, my opening credits were soundtracked by Rosé's "On The Ground," which suggests my movie was less of a rom-com and more of an existential coming-of-age drama.

It has been revealed that what made this feature so charming was how it leaned into something music lovers already did: imagine elaborate cinematic scenarios while listening to their favorite songs. Anyone who's ever stared wistfully out of a train window with their headphones on knows exactly what I'm talking about.

In a recent development, spotify understood the assignment with this one. Bring it back! — CB.

Of all the ways Spotify could have visualized your top five music genres, it chose lunch.

Sources indicate that in 2023, Spotify Wrapped served up a personalized genre sandwich, with each of your five most-listened-to genres represented by a colorful layer between two pieces of bread. The thickness of each layer reflected how much you listened to that genre relative to the others.

Industry observers note that according to Spotify's global marketing team, the sandwich was chosen because it was globally recognizable and easily customizable. There were even different types of bread.

Sources indicate that spotify committed to the bit, too. The tech giant teamed up with viral Brooklyn deli owner Rahim Mohamed, better known online as General Ock, to make an actual sandwich inspired by New York City's five most-streamed genres that year: pop, hip-hop, rock, indie, and Latin.

Was a sandwich the most intuitive way to visualize a year's worth of listening data? Probably not. But there was something delightfully absurd about telling your friends that your music taste consisted of a thick slab of K-pop, a generous helping of indie rock, and a thin slice of emo.

According to recent reports, personally, I'd like to know what sauce pairs best with existential synth-pop. — CB.

Crystal Bell is the Digital Culture Editor at Mashable, where she leads coverage of the creator economy, internet culture, and digital life. Her work focuses on the people, platforms, and communities shaping modern entertainment, from YouTube creators and livestreamers to fandoms, social media trends, and the evolving relationship between technology and culture. She also oversees the Mashable 101, the publication's annual list recognizing the internet's most influential creators.

According to recent reports, previously, she was the entertainment director at MTV News, where she helped expand the brand's coverage of fan culture, K-pop, and the internet's most passionate communities. Her work has appeared in Teen Vogue, Rolling Stone, PAPER, NYLON, ELLE, Glamour, NME, W, The FADER, and elsewhere on the internet.

She's exceptionally fluent in fandom and will gladly make you a K-pop playlist and/or provide anime recommendations upon request. Crystal lives in Upcoming York City with her two black cats, Howl and Sophie.

Industry observers note that olivia Tauber is the deputy editor of digital culture, covering creators, media, movies, beauty, and more. Based in New York, her work has appeared in The New York Times, Vanity Fair, The Cut, Teen Vogue, Complex, and Interview Magazine. She holds a Master's degree in Journalism from NYU and a Bachelor's from the University of Michigan. She also runs Fan Mail, a weekly pop-culture newsletter.

EA adds AI-generated John Motson to FC 27 video game

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • John Motson was a legendary football commentator who covered 10 World Cups, 10 European Championships and 29 FA Cup finals for BBC Sport.
  • Football game EA Sports FC will feature the digitally recreated voice of the late commentator John Motson, Electronic Arts has exclusively told the BBC.
  • Motson, who died in 2023, was the main commentator for BBC Sport for decades - and performed the same role for the video game series during the 90s and 00s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

John Motson was a legendary football commentator who covered 10 World Cups, 10 European Championships and 29 FA Cup finals for BBC Sport.

Football game EA Sports FC will feature the digitally recreated voice of the late commentator John Motson, Electronic Arts has exclusively told the BBC.

Motson, who died in 2023, was the main commentator for BBC Sport for decades - and performed the same role for the video game series during the 90s and 00s.

It is the first time the hit series, formerly known as Fifa, has featured a deceased commentator.

With the permission of his widow and his son, Motson's voice has been synthesised using a combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. It will become available in FC 27 on 26 November.

The legendary commentator died aged 77 in February 2023 - several months after the launch of ChatGPT and the massive growth of AI it set in train.

Fred Motson told the BBC it "means an awful lot" to have his dad's voice in EA Sports FC once again.

In a recent development, "I grew up with Fifa," he said. "I always used to tell my parents that I needed the latest console for Christmas because otherwise dad couldn't see how the game worked.".

Electronic Arts, which was bought for $55bn (Â£42bn) in August, told the BBC it paid Motson's family for the rights to use his likeness and recreate his voice, but would not disclose the financial terms of the deal.

The BBC's lead football commentator Guy Mowbray remarked it was a "privilege" to be involved in the game, which he has provided commentary for since 2023.

"I think it's quite a nice, sort of non-scary use of AI," he stated.

According to recent reports, "We're in the business of nostalgia... I hear commentary not in my own voice, but in John's voice, because that's the voice I knew growing up.

"So I think it's nice that that legacy can be continued in this way.".

WATCH: The newly introduced John Motson commentary in EA Sports FC 27 - and how it sounded back in Fifa 1998.

It has been revealed that john Motson was the first commentator for the series, appearing on games from Fifa 96 up to Fifa 2005. He later made a brief cameo in Fifa 19.

"While he completely understood when they went in a different direction, I think he really missed it after he left the game and it felt like a bit of an end of an era," his son stated.

EA told the BBC the studio would not have included Motson in the game unless they had permission from his family.

"There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," stated Mat Prior, senior game design director at EA Sports FC.

"At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back.".

He explained that Motson's voice in the game was a combination of old lines he recorded over the years and AI - tech which he remarked was "the only way" to make it happen, as they don't have recordings of him talking about modern players like Bradley Barcola and Chloe Kelly.

Gazza's tears, Radford's screamer & the Crazy Gang - 5 of Motty's best.

Motson's son Fred remarked he believed his dad would have "absolutely" wanted to be involved in the game after his death.

In a recent development, "My dad was the least technological person in the world," he stated. "Till his dying day, he had a typewriter on his desk.

"So I don't think he would have quite understood what the AI was doing technologically - but I think, on the other hand, he was always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects.".

But Peter Caulfield, founder of Save Our Voices Now which campaigns against AI voice cloning, expressed some disquiet about the project, and the fact Motson had been unable to consent to it.

"If someone has signed a deal allowing their likeness to be used after they die, I have no problem with that," he said.

"But in life or in death, unless you have specifically agreed to it, AI cloning of any kind should not be allowed.

"Being a family member shouldn't automatically give you that right either.".

One of the main arguments against the use of generative AI in video games is that it can replace humans - something that EA was keen to argue against.

"From a gaming standpoint, it's something we've used for many years - like machine learning to help drive animation systems and so on and so forth," Prior said.

"It's not there to replace commentators in any way shape or form... there's certainly no future intends to replace anyone with AI.".

Derek Rae, who has been a commentator in EA FC for several years, stated the tech could make things easier, but he still spent a long time recording dialogue in studios.

"It's quite a lot of days in the course of a year," he stated. "So it might be two or three times a month that we do it in season for the game, which is typically sort of November time through until May.

"The more creative things have to be done with the human voice because they have to have the personality, sometimes a little chuckle thrown in the middle of a sentence or a little idiosyncrasy," he noted.

"But when it comes to the more normal features in a video game, for example, routine surnames like Smith and Jones and Brown, that's something that AI can probably accomplish quite easily.".

Josko Gvardiol tackling Jamal Musiala in FC 27 - perhaps examples of some less routine surnames.

Rae said he was excited about the Motson project - but wasn't convinced he would follow suit.

"If we're being modest, we might say, well, no, I don't want to inflict my voice on the next generation.".

He told BBC News it was something he would need to "think about" it but added: "I'm hopefully many years away from having to make a decision like that.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that connecticut's online casino revenue reached a fresh high in October 2026, the first month taxed at a higher rate.
  • According to recent reports, connecticut’s two online casino operators, DraftKings and FanDuel, beat the previous record of $59.7 million, set in March, by about 10%.
  • Sources indicate that wagering grew as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that connecticut's online casino revenue reached a fresh high in October 2026, the first month taxed at a higher rate. Growth in the state sped up while the national market has been cooling.

According to recent reports, connecticut’s two online casino operators, DraftKings and FanDuel, beat the previous record of $59.7 million, set in March, by about 10%. October revenue was also nearly $10 million higher than September’s total.

Sources indicate that wagering grew as well. Online casino handle topped $2 billion for the first time and was up 10% from October 2025. Revenue grew faster than handle in the month. That is consistent with operators keeping a larger share of each dollar wagered.

In a recent development, the October result runs against a cooling national picture. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in Q3 2026, the slowest rate on record, SiGMA World reported. Connecticut grew at that same 12% pace in the quarter.

According to recent reports, the American Gaming Association’s tracker reveals US iGaming revenue hit a record $3.05 billion in Q3 2026, up 13.5%. That was still the slowest quarterly growth since 2018. Connecticut had been part of the stronger phase. Its iGaming revenue reached $707.5 million in 2025, a 31.7% increase from 2024.

Sources indicate that the jump from single-digit growth in September to a new high a month later stands out. It suggests the national slowdown is not uniform across states. One month, however, does not set a trend.

Operators paid the state 18% of online casino gross gaming revenue through September 2026. They owe 20% for every period after that, the Department of Consumer Protection’s dataset notes show. That lower rate covered the five years after online casino gaming began on October 12, 2021.

In a recent development, the state’s take was already sizable before the increase. Online casino operators paid Connecticut $108,265,925 in 2025. Operators can still deduct some promotional credits before tax. That deduction has been capped at 15% of win since October 2023.

Industry observers note that october’s figures show the higher rate did not coincide with any immediate drop in revenue. That matters for other states weighing online casino tax rates. It also matters for the two operators, which now share a larger tax bill in a market they split almost evenly.

Connecticut online casino wagers passed $2 billion in October, a record, in the first month taxed at 20% rather than 18%, according to state data. pic.twitter.com/FpO6DdEDUU.

— iGaming Times (@igaming_times) November 19, 2026.

October was only the second month in the past 12 in which DraftKings, rather than FanDuel, took the larger share of Connecticut online casino revenue, according to Poker Industry PRO. FanDuel has led the state in most months over that period.

In a recent development, operators must send each month’s online casino payment to the state by the 15th of the following month. The first payment at the 20% rate was due by November 15, 2026. Payments on November revenue fall due by the 15th of December.

Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy to step down next week amid IPO uncertainty

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above), who steered Flipkart through Walmart’s acquisition in 2018 and helped build it into one of India’s biggest e-commerce companies, is stepping down as chief executive next week after more than 11 years with the organization.
  • On Wednesday, Flipkart said it would announce Krishnamurthy’s successor in the coming weeks, and Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan will lead the firm until a replacement is found.
  • A Walmart spokesperson told TechCrunch that Krishnamurthy’s last day at Flipkart will be December 4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above), who steered Flipkart through Walmart’s acquisition in 2018 and helped build it into one of India’s biggest e-commerce companies, is stepping down as chief executive next week after more than 11 years with the organization.

On Wednesday, Flipkart said it would announce Krishnamurthy’s successor in the coming weeks, and Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan will lead the firm until a replacement is found.

A Walmart spokesperson told TechCrunch that Krishnamurthy’s last day at Flipkart will be December 4.

Industry observers note that krishnamurthy joined Flipkart in 2015 from Tiger Global, one of the company’s early investors, and became its CEO in 2017. He remained at the helm after Walmart acquired a controlling stake in the company for $16 billion in 2018.

Industry observers note that under Krishnamurthy, Flipkart remarked its business grew more than five-fold. The firm has more than 500 million registered users and over 1.4 million sellers, including those on Shopsy, its low-cost shopping platform. The company’s marketplace offers over 150 million products across more than 80 categories.

Recent findings suggest that flipkart has of late moved into newer segments, including quick-commerce through Flipkart Minutes and, more recently, food delivery through a venture called Eat-in by Minutes. The expansion is targeted at Indian consumers who are increasingly turning to quick-delivery services for everything from groceries to electronics.

It has been revealed that thiagarajan joined Flipkart in September last year to lead its product and technology teams. Before that, he had founded Kasu.ai, a Bay Area startup working on AI assistants for corporate finance. He also previously worked at Google, Microsoft, and Uber in senior engineering positions, per his LinkedIn profile.

Krishnamurthy’s exit comes amid uncertainty around Flipkart’s IPO. In March, the organization moved its headquarters from Singapore to India as part of its preparations to go public, but in May, Walmart reportedly told Flipkart to delay its IPO and focus on becoming profitable first.

Recent findings suggest that walmart declined to comment beyond its announcement when asked what prompted Krishnamurthy’s departure, and whether the leadership change would affect Flipkart’s IPO plans. Flipkart did not respond to a request for comment.

Founded in 2007 by Sachin and Binny Bansal as an online bookstore, much like its bigger rival Amazon, Flipkart eventually expanded into other categories. Under Krishnamurthy, it has grown into India’s largest online retailer by gross merchandise value, ahead of Amazon.

It has been revealed that “Both Flipkart and Walmart are better because of Kalyan. We are grateful for his leadership, the governance he instilled and his many contributions to the company,” Chris Nicholas, president and CEO, Walmart International, said in a statement.

  • Recent findings suggest that panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Recent findings suggest that panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” notes Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”.

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.

In a recent development, the US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

Sources indicate that this is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”.

According to recent reports, her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” claims Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the firm has preferential pricing for agencies.

Sources indicate that the newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The manufacturer describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”.

Sources indicate that while incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, Newly introduced York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she claims. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.

It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a Upcoming York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.

It has been revealed that in Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” notes Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button matter, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.

Industry observers note that while more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.

Recent findings suggest that on the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”.

According to recent reports, as volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she indicates, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”.

Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.

Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich states the fresh rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”.

Sources indicate that fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” states Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.

Industry observers note that kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.

Industry observers note that startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” indicates Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.

Sources indicate that as states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” claims Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buying a new TV is always a massive decision, namely because its a big piece of tech with a permanent place in your home that you'll be staring at for hours on end. Not to mention, some of the best of the best cost thousands of dollars. It doesn't help that most TVs look exactly the same and have nondescript names like the Samsung S95H—not great for narrowing your options.

Fear not. After stress-testing multiple TVs this year, I can attest to one simple truth: in 2026, you have more great options than ever. Art TVs and RGB TVs exploded onto the market and made the typical “just buy an OLED TV” advice seem like an ancient relic of a bygone. These top-performing televisions are my “desert island” picks, if said island had a power generator and good popcorn.

For more audio and home theater recommendations, check out related guides to the best OLED TVs, the best art TVs, the best RGB TVs, the best home theater projectors, and the best soundbars. If you truly don't know where to start, try our guide on how to buy a TV.

Update November 2026: We've revamped this entire guide, replacing nearly all of our top picks, Honorable Mentions, and Other TVs We've Tested.

The great debate: which size television is best for your living room? Does it even matter? The first thing to consider is price: an 80-inch TV is going to cost significantly more than a 65-inch one. In some cases, that means an extra grand or two for the privilege of seeing the stubble on Spider-Man’s face in great detail. Broadly speaking, the larger the room, the more useful a large screen is. The most popular size is 65 inches, which is a great option for most medium sizes spaces.

I’m partial to art televisions for one simple reason: They are useful even when they are turned off. Art TVs use an antireflective layer on top of the screen to create more realistic, textured still images like artwork or paintings. The best ones can replace a picture frame or wall art in any room, and double as great TVs.

Should You Pick an OLED or RGB TV?

TV tech has evolved in 2026, and the new kid on the block is RGB TVs. These new models shine red, blue, and green light through an LCD panel to create brighter, more vibrant color. OLED on the other hand can control the color of individual pixels and even turn them off completely, leading to excellent contrast and black levels.

Sources indicate that which one performs the best? That depends. RGB models like the LG Micro RGB Evo provide more control over picture quality, brightness, and contrast. OLED televisions like the Samsung S95H tend to look better on movie night, especially for nighttime scenes when inky blacks need to look realistic. If pressed, I’d pick an RGB TV model because you get more control over color, but that's just me.

Samsung The Frame Pro (2026) Specs.

According to recent reports, I picked Samsung's The Frame Pro (2026) as the best overall TV because it has stunningly good picture quality and looks incredible showcasing a masterpiece painting on your wall. I remember staring at the 65-inch model on the wall of my office for two months, just marveling at high-res shipwreck photos and the real wood bezels that encompass the screen (and snap easily into place, by the way). With just about every painting, The Frame Pro showed intricate and detailed textures, as though you could reach out and feel the waves of an ocean or curve of a face.

According to recent reports, the Frame Pro is also an excellent choice for movies and shows. Because of the anti-glare screen and matte finish, the dark corridors of scenes in The Batman on HBO had extra depth and animated movies like Toy Story 5 on Disney+ popped with color. Sure, it doesn't have the true black pixels of an OLED screen, but its other capabilities more than make up for it.

In a recent development, extra features included easy-to-install stands (no screws needed) and a breakout box called the Samsung Wireless One Connect that lets you connect streaming devices and a game console from across the room. That means fewer wires dangling on the wall.

TCL is a more budget-focused television maker that tends to undercut the price of brands like Samsung and LG. A good example of this is the TCL QM7L Mini-LED TV above, which has a budget-friendly price but anything but oriented picture quality. If anything, this QLED model competes with some OLED TVs for inky, deep blacks and rich color. Will you notice any contrast problems when you watch the latest Pixar film? Probably not, especially since the QM7L also looked exceptionally bright in our tests.

A few other extras to mention: We loved the backlit remote, which makes it easier to punch up the volume or adjust picture quality settings in a dark room. You might even be able to skip a soundbar with this TV—the internal Bang & Olufsen speakers sound nice and loud.

Samsung, TCL, Hisense, and Sony released new RGB TVs this year, but it's the LG Micro RGB Evo that takes the crown, namely because you can tweak so many of its picture settings. In my tests,I could tweak the picture so much that movies and shows that mostly take place at night still looked visible, clear, and realistic. As one example among many, I remember tweaking settings for the movie Awake, a largely dark film, to the point where it looked clear and colorful. Other RGB models from Hisense and even Samsung struggled with those same dark scenes, no matter which setting I used.

Recent findings suggest that another major plus is that this model supports 100 percent of the color gamut specs for BT.2020, DCI-P3, and Adobe RGB. In layman's terms, if you watch a movie like Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (which also matches those specs), you will see a true rainbow of every color available, with unmatched color vibrancy. This TV is so striking that I came away thinking that OLED TVs are no longer the obvious gold standard in 2026.

Sources indicate that samsung made a big change to their flagship OLED model this year, the Samsung S95H. They ditch the Samsung One Connect breakout box that was required with previous models (and is still required on TVs like The Frame Pro). The TV now has ports directly on the panel, where you can connect video game consoles, streaming devices, or Blu-ray players directly. While that might create more cable clutter, I found it much easier to use than the previous Samsung S95F.

According to recent reports, perhaps more importantly, the S95H is a top performer when it comes to picture quality and settings. I could adjust the contrast and brightness to perfectly light famously dim indicates like Game of Thrones. As an OLED, the blacks look richer and darker, more so than most RGB models. The AI optimization picture settings here are actually useful—during soccer matches, the TV adjust to make the pitch look even greener and minimizes background crowd noise, for example.

It's a bit pricey, but the overall brightness, contrast, color quality, and even built-in sound are all premium-grade.

The organization famous for streaming sticks released its first OLED TV this year, and it follows the brand's formula of low-cost simplicity. Roku has, up until this point, stuck with LED TV models with average performance. Wonder of wonders, the Pro Series is not bad at all, making even dark scenes in movies like Solo: A Star Wars Story look vibrant and colorful. Outside of picture quality, Roku makes things as easy as possible, with features like Smart Picture Max, which automatically tweaks picture settings for you, a simple TV operating system (Roku OS, of course), and an uncluttered remote.

I will say, the brightness and contrast are good for this price, but nowhere near the cinema-quality color of something like the premium Samsung S95H. I think it's a great option for anyone on a budget or for people who only watch TV occasionally.

Industry observers note that the Samsung The Frame Pro (2026) is my TV of the year, but the Amazon Ember Artline is also a capable, significantly cheaper, art TV. Just don't expert as premium of an image in movies and TV demonstrates.

Art televisions use a matte finish on the screen to help make paintings look more realistic and textured. The Ember Artline achieves this look, and even includes frame bezel that snap into place around the screen (these are sold separately on Samsung's Frame TVs). I loved looking at painting on this TV, including some animated ones Amazon offers in the catalog. Using the TV is simple, and the improved Alexa+ voice assistant is useful for changing the volume (hands free) or finding obscure sci-fi films.

Recent findings suggest that image quality isn't the big selling point of this TV: the art, aesthetic, and low price are. Gamers will find the 60 Hz refresh rate lacking, especially for twitchy action titles. Contrast and brightness are okay, but not nearly as impressive as something like the Samsung The Frame Pro. But keep in mind: this TV is far, far cheaper than premium options.

While the LG Micro RGB Evo is endlessly tweakable and outperformed every other RGB model I tested for picture quality, the Sony BRAVIA 9 II RGB TV still takes the cake when it comes to gaming. That’s especially true if you own a Sony PlayStation 5, since the TV will automatically adjust the picture quality and latency to match the game console. I tested it mostly using a high-end PC, and at a 120 Hz refresh rate, latency felt non-existent to me.

I also found this TV to be a capable alternative to a premium OLED. Red, green, and blue colors are almost infinitely adjustable. During a scene in Toy Story 5 by a tree in a field, the sun creates splashes of color that look incredibly lush and vivid. Watching Game of Thrones, I found I could enable a special black level setting to make night battles look more realistic.

It has been revealed that the Bravia 9 II uses Google TV OS and Google Gemini voice assistant, which both run simply, smoothly, and with no weird hiccups. While the LG Micro RGB Evo is a better performer for color and contrast, the BRAVIA 9 II’s gaming features, fast performance, high-end speakers, and deep blacks are exceptional.

Industry observers note that hisense UR9 RGB Mini-LED: My top pick for a midrange RGB, the Hisense UR9 has rich colors thanks to RGB tech shining red, green, and blue pixels. Some scenes, including ones in the movie The Last Duel, looked extra crisp and colorful. But it's not quite as excellent as my top picks.

LG B6 OLED: The LG B6 is a great budget-friendly OLED TV that performed very similarly to the Roku Pro Series OLED. Either one of them would serve you well, but we gave the nod to the Roku TV for it's lower price, simpler remote, and easy to use Roku operating system.

According to recent reports, samsung Micro RGB R95H: Samsung's Micro RGB display tech didn’t make the Samsung Micro RGB R95H stand out from the competition as much as I'd hoped. In fact, the LG Micro RGB Evo responded much better to picture quality adjustments, and while shows and movies looked colorful and clear, they weren't quite as jaw-dropping as similarly priced RGB and OLED competitors.

Recent findings suggest that sony Bravia 7 II: The Sony Bravia 7 II is unfortunately outclassed by the other midrange RGB TV on this list: the Hisense UR9. It is more expensive, it's harder to set up, and the picture quality doesn't quite match that of the Hisense TV.

Sony Bravia 8 II: Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata tested this stunning high-end OLED, and praised it's top-notch image quality and processing. That stated, the Samsung S95H is newer, about the same price, and has a more striking, glare-free image than the Sony Bravia 8 II.

Sources indicate that TCL Nxtvision Series Art: This budget art TV simply cannot compete with similarly low-priced art TVs like the Amazon Ember Artline TV and Hisense Class S7 CanvasTV. Both offer better picture quality and a better general user experience. You can read my full review here.

Sources indicate that finally, there’s the Daily Forecast section that gives you an eight-day overview via a temperature-range layout, which is my favorite way to visualize this information. Again, this can be tapped to get a bottom sheet explorer.

According to recent reports, I've lost count on how many weather apps on Android I've tried out over the years but since the Pixel Weather app became a thing I've tried far fewer and the few I have tried while many have been prettier to look at, I've always ended up coming back to the stock PW app. It never hurts to have options though and this one looks like a good one. The Radar tab is up next, with Google Maps powering this view. From the three-dot overflow menu, you can customize the Animation Speed, Map Layers, Style, and Options.

Sources indicate that settings is where you can make all the aforementioned customizations, including changing which Forecast Data source you’re using. The usual players are here, like The Weather Channel and AccuWeather. I also like the stylized in-app changelog.

In a recent development, in Notifications, you can have a persistent silent alert appear. There’s also the ability to receive Morning and Evening Reports, along with Precipitation and Severe Alerts. This is joined by a trio of homescreen widgets.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A bill now sponsored by Wyoming's Legislative Management Council would make running a dual-currency sweepstakes casino a felony.
  • According to recent reports, wyoming is moving to outlaw dual-currency sweepstakes casinos.
  • It has been revealed that the gaming committee indicates casino-style sweepstakes games are already available in Wyoming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A bill now sponsored by Wyoming's Legislative Management Council would make running a dual-currency sweepstakes casino a felony. The draft also targets the vendors behind these sites, which raises the legal risk for payment processors and B2B suppliers.

According to recent reports, wyoming is moving to outlaw dual-currency sweepstakes casinos. Its bill reaches past operators to the companies that keep them running. The draft reached the Legislative Management Council through Sen. John Kolb, co-chair of the Select Committee on Gaming. The council also agreed to sponsor two other gaming bills, one on pari-mutuel wagering breakage and one on background checks.

It has been revealed that the gaming committee indicates casino-style sweepstakes games are already available in Wyoming. These games let players wager with currency redeemable for money or prizes. The draft would state that the state’s prize-promotion laws do not authorize them. People who take part only as players are exempt.

Working draft 0.4 widens the definition of professional gambling. It covers anyone who knowingly provides services to an online sweepstakes game. Those services include geolocation, payment processing, hosting, game content and advertising. Vendors and processors would carry legal risk, not only the brands that face players.

Sources indicate that the approach follows Oklahoma. Under SB 1589, companies that provide geolocation or payment services to a sweepstakes operator after November 1 face the same felony charges as the operator. Oklahoma lawmakers overrode Gov. Kevin Stitt’s veto of that bill. The votes were 34-10 in the Senate and 68-19 in the House.

It has been revealed that complaints to the regulator help explain the push. Wyoming Gaming Commission Executive Director Nick Larramendy described his office’s complaint load to lawmakers. Sweepstakes complaints arrive each week in greater numbers than complaints about any regulated form of gaming. Most come from players whose accounts were shut down when they tried to cash out a jackpot. The operators are often offshore, where the commission cannot reach them.

Taking such sites down would be easier with the ban in place, in Larramendy’s view, because the commission would have firmer ground for working with the Department of Justice and internet service providers. His testimony also pointed to a well-known payment processor. It serves offshore sweepstakes sites while holding a Wyoming online sports betting permit.

The bill has drawn broad support at each step. At its October 5-6 meeting, the gaming committee voted 6-0 in a roll call to recommend the amended draft. It also renamed the bill ‘Online sweepstakes prohibited.’ Lawmakers weighed a rival draft, 27LSO-0200, which would have regulated sweepstakes rather than banned them. Only the prohibition draft went to the council.

Sources indicate that A sweepstakes ban bill in Pennsylvania has stalled. Rep. Russ Diamond introduced HB 2801 on September 24. The bill has had no hearing or vote in the House Gaming Oversight Committee. The state’s legislative session ends November 30.

Wyoming’s draft is written as a Senate File. It now goes to the 2027 General Session, which is scheduled to begin January 12, 2027. A general session can last no more than 40 legislative days. If passed, the ban would take effect July 1, 2027.

Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store.

The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse people discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.

According to a Wednesday report by Fortune, citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter.

Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported.

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered "signals" that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, chatbots are making it easier for individuals to file requests.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests. That could potentially make public offices less transparent.

Find out how AI is testing the limits of America's right to know.

Recent findings suggest that their probe revealed an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases. Now, researchers are trying to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking?
